file: papers/pdf/Brown - 2005 - Science Serendipity and the Contemporary Marketing Condition.pdf
about: A viewpoint commentary arguing that luck and serendipity play a significant part in business and marketing success, that luck can be partly made through belief and a prepared mind, and that marketing should take serendipity seriously rather than fixating on customer orientation.

candidates.label: Chance encounter or conversation
candidates.definition: An unplanned meeting or conversation with someone, often from outside one's field, that resolves a problem or opens a new direction.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes an accidental meeting or casual conversation (e.g., at a social event) that sparked a new idea or course of action.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The meeting was deliberately sought out for that purpose.

candidates.label: Unexpected anomaly or side-effect
candidates.definition: An anomalous event, unanticipated result or incongruous finding, such as a side-effect discovered while searching for something else, that becomes the basis of success.
candidates.applies_when: The person reports that while pursuing one goal they encountered an unexpected result that they then exploited.

candidates.label: Happening to be in the right place
candidates.definition: Success arising simply because the actor happened to be present or positioned somewhere at the right time, rather than through systematic analysis.
candidates.applies_when: The account attributes a discovery or opportunity to coincidental presence or timing (e.g., a rig happening to be in the area, a visit that revealed a technology).
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Presence resulted from painstaking analysis or planned search.

candidates.label: Idea out of the blue
candidates.definition: An idea that comes suddenly and unbidden, sometimes in an incidental setting, and is developed very quickly.
candidates.applies_when: The person describes a sudden inspiration or whim that arrived unexpectedly and launched a product or venture.

candidates.label: Recognising significance of the accident
candidates.definition: Turning a chance occurrence into something requires noticing and appreciating its significance rather than discarding the unusual as inconsequential.
candidates.applies_when: The account shows the person noticing that an accidental event mattered and acting on it instead of dismissing it.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The person encountered the accident but ignored or dismissed it.

candidates.label: Prepared mind
candidates.definition: Training, reading, research and experience that enable a person to appreciate the significance of serendipitous occurrences; chance favours the prepared mind.
candidates.applies_when: The person links their ability to spot or use a lucky event to prior knowledge, expertise or experience.

candidates.label: Rigid adherence to preconceived plan
candidates.definition: The unprepared mind, or one socialised into normal practice, discards the unusual because it does not conform to the preconceived plan, so serendipity is overlooked.
candidates.applies_when: The account describes ignoring or rejecting an unexpected input because it did not fit plans or established ways of thinking.

candidates.label: Believing oneself lucky
candidates.definition: Those who believe they are lucky and act on that belief find their luck increases, while those expecting bad luck often get it; luck can be made, caught or created.
candidates.applies_when: The person expresses expecting good fortune or seeing themselves as lucky and acting accordingly, linked to good outcomes.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Luck is described as wholly uncontrollable and external.

candidates.label: Founding or redirecting a venture by chance
candidates.definition: Chance events can found ventures or redirect careers and enterprises, such that without them the trajectory would have been entirely different.
candidates.applies_when: The account presents a chance event as the origin of a business or as changing its or the person's direction.

candidates.label: Major commercial success from luck
candidates.definition: Serendipity and sheer good fortune are a significant factor in commercial success, enormous fortunes and breakthrough products.
candidates.applies_when: The person attributes significant success, growth or a breakthrough product partly to luck.

candidates.label: Planning and analysis as explanation
candidates.definition: Conventional accounts explain success through analysis, planning, control and customer orientation, treating luck as nonexistent or an uncontrollable external factor; the author criticises this.
candidates.applies_when: The account attributes outcomes entirely to deliberate planning, rational management or strategy.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Planning is acknowledged alongside a chance element.

candidates.label: Success-equals-customer-satisfaction inference
candidates.definition: Inferring customer orientation from success is fallacious; success may instead stem from lack of alternatives, competitor ineptitude, shortages or sheer good fortune.
candidates.applies_when: Success is explained post hoc as proof of meeting customer needs, or alternative causes like competitor weakness are offered.

candidates.label: Partly fluke, partly foresight
candidates.definition: Retrospective accounts that apportion success between luck and foresight, acknowledging that fluke played a large part.
candidates.applies_when: The person narrates success as a mix of luck and foresight, or admits it was largely a fluke or whim.
